unesco-1995.label: verified
unesco-1995.says: The historic centre of Naples was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1995.
quote: Date of Inscription: 1995
was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1995

name.label: supported
name.says: Spaccanapoli, literally 'Naples splitter', is an unofficial name; officially the street is Via Benedetto Croce and Via San Biagio dei Librai.
quote: Notice that Spaccanapoli (literally "Naples splitter") is an unofficial name. The street's official names are Via Benedetto Croce for its western part and Via San Biagio Dei Librai for its eastern section.

sc-street.label: supported
sc-street.says: Santa Chiara faces Via Benedetto Croce.
quote: The basilica church of Santa Chiara faces Via Benedetto Croce

square.label: supported
square.says: The Gesù Nuovo square holds the church of Gesù Nuovo, the church of Santa Chiara and the spire of the Immaculate Virgin.
quote: Three notable landmarks can be found in the Gesù Nuovo square:
The Church of Santa Chiara;
The spire (guglia) of the Immaculate Virgin

guglia.label: supported
guglia.says: The Guglia dell'Immacolata, in front of Gesù Nuovo, is the tallest and most ornate of three plague columns in Naples; begun in the 17th century, finished only in 1750.
quote: The Guglia dell'Immacolata is a monument that stands in the square in front of the church of Gesù Nuovo. It is the tallest and most ornamental of three such "plague columns" in Naples.
Begun in the 17th century, it was completed only in 1750 after decades of pauses in construction.

guglia-why.label: tradition
guglia-why.says: It is said to have been built to ask the Virgin Mary's protection from the plague.
quote: Putatively, it was built to invoke the Virgin Mary's protection from the plague.

gesu-palace.label: supported
gesu-palace.says: Gesù Nuovo began as a palace built in 1470 for Roberto Sanseverino, Prince of Salerno; after the family's political intrigues it was confiscated and sold in the 1580s to the Jesuits for 45,000 ducats, who built the church from 1584 to 1601.
quote: The Church of Gesù Nuovo was originally a palace built in 1470 for Roberto Sanseverino, Prince of Salerno.

Political intrigues by the Sanseverino family caused the property to be confiscated, and eventually sold in the 1580s to the Jesuits for 45,000 ducats to construct a church (1584–1601) under architect Giuseppe Valeriano.

gesu-facade.label: supported
gesu-facade.says: The church kept the palace's unusual front, faced with diamond-shaped stone projections.
quote: The new church retained the unusual facade, originally built for the palace, faced with rustic ashlar diamond projections.
The unusual façade, unusually plain for a Baroque style church, is of rusticated ashlar and is the original façade of the palace.

gesu-solimena.label: supported
gesu-solimena.says: On the inside of the front wall is The Expulsion of Heliodorus from the Temple (1725) by Francesco Solimena.
quote: At the back of the facade is The Expulsion of Heliodorus from the Temple (1725), a baroque masterpiece by Francesco Solimena.

moscati.label: supported
moscati.says: Under the altar of the chapel of the Visitation lie the remains of St Joseph Moscati (1880-1927), a university teacher and head physician of the Incurabili hospital, canonized in 1987 by Pope John Paul II.
quote: The chapel of the Visitation has an altar-piece by Massimo Stanzione. Under the altar there is a bronze urn containing the mortal remains of St. Joseph Moscati (1880–1927), a biochemistry teacher at the University of Naples and head physician of the Ospedale degli Incurabili, canonized on 25 October 1987 by Pope John Paul II.

sc-built.label: disputed
sc-built.says: Santa Chiara was built by King Robert of Naples and Queen Sancha of Majorca; one account gives 1313-1340, another 1310-1328.
quote: The double monastic complex was built in 1313–1340 by Queen Sancha of Majorca and her husband King Robert of Naples
The Church of Santa Chiara is a Gothic style church-convent built between 1310 and 1328 for the wife of Robert, King of Naples.

sc-largest.label: supported
sc-largest.says: Santa Chiara was the largest church of the Poor Clares (Clarissan) ever built.
quote: Santa Chiara was the largest Clarissan church ever built

sc-wall.label: supported
sc-wall.says: Behind the altar is King Robert's tomb, and behind that a wall hiding the nuns' choir, with three screened grilles through which the nuns watched Mass unseen.
quote: Behind the altar is the tomb of King Robert, behind that is a wall separating the main body of the church from the nuns' choir.
The wall between the nave of the church and the retrochoir is penetrated by three screened grilles through which the nuns could observe the mass, while being invisible to anybody in the nave.

sc-robert-tomb.label: supported
sc-robert-tomb.says: King Robert of Anjou's tomb behind the main altar was sculpted by Pacio and Giovanni Bertini in 1343.
quote: Behind the main altar is the tomb of King Robert of Anjou, which was sculpted by Pacio and Giovanni Bertini in 1343.

sc-war.label: supported
sc-war.says: Allied bombing in 1943 and the fire that followed wrecked the church; a disputed restoration to its supposed original Gothic state was completed in 1953.
quote: After the edifice was partially destroyed by a fire after the Allied bombings during World War II, it was brought back to the alleged original state by a disputed restoration, which was completed in 1953.
Unfortunately much of the interior decoration was destroyed in the aerial bombardment of 1943.

sc-rebirth.label: supported
sc-rebirth.says: Rebuilding Santa Chiara became the symbol of the rebirth of Naples.
quote: The symbol of the rebirth of Naples was the rebuilding of the church of Santa Chiara

sc-dacquisto.label: supported
sc-dacquisto.says: The side chapels hold the tombs of King Francis II and Queen Maria Sophie, and of the national hero Salvo D'Acquisto, a carabiniere who gave his life to save 22 civilian hostages during the Nazi occupation.
quote: In the side chapels are the tombs of the Bourbon king of Naples, Francis II and his consort Maria Sophie of Bavaria, as well as those of Queen Maria Christina of Savoy and of the national hero Salvo D'Acquisto (a carabiniere who sacrificed his life to save the lives of 22 civilian hostages during the Nazi occupation).

sc-cloister.label: supported
sc-cloister.says: The nuns' cloister was covered with majolica tiles in 1742 by Domenico Antonio Vaccaro; bright floral decoration on octagonal columns that seems to clash with the enclosed life of the nuns.
quote: The cloister of the Clarisses is known for the unique addition of majolica tiles, added in 1742 by Domenico Antonio Vaccaro in Rococò style. The brash color floral decoration makes this cloister, with octagonal columns in pergola-like structure, likely unique and would seem to clash with the introspective world of cloistered nuns.

sc-rear.label: supported
sc-rear.says: The cloister is at the rear of the church.
quote: The noteworthy monastic courtyard at the rear of the church

grid.label: verified
grid.says: The rectangular grid of Greek Neapolis can still be traced and still gives the old centre its basic shape.
quote: The rectangular grid layout of the ancient Greek foundation of Neapolis is still discernible and has indeed continued to provide the basic form for the present-day urban fabric of the Historic Centre of Naples
The rectangular grid layout of the ancient Greek foundation of Neapolis is still discernible.

maze.label: supported
maze.says: The old centre is full of small irregular alleys; Spaccanapoli and Via dei Tribunali are long, narrow, crowded east-west streets packed with vendors and old churches.
quote: filled with small irregular alleys
Via dei Tribunali and Spaccanapoli are two long, but rather narrow and crowded roads crossing the centre from east to west, both packed with street vendors and old churches.

founding.label: disputed
founding.says: UNESCO dates the refounding as Neapolis, the New City, to 470 BC, after an older settlement called Parthenope; Wikipedia puts the refounding in the sixth century BC.
quote: Its origins go back to its foundation as Parthenope or Palaepolis in the 9th century B.C., subsequently re-established as Neapolis (New City) in 470 B.C.
In the sixth century BC, it was refounded as Neápolis.

history-2700.label: supported
history-2700.says: The historic centre is the oldest part of the city, with a history of over 2,700 years.
quote: is the oldest part of the city, with a history that spans over 2,700 years.

walls-height.label: supported
walls-height.says: In the Middle Ages building outside the city walls was forbidden, so the old centre grew upward rather than outward.
quote: In this context the city was closed by its walls beyond which there was an absolute prohibition of construction.
is the almost foreclosure of the development in extension of the city, thus favoring that "in height".

quarries.label: supported
quarries.says: Naples sits on tuff; building stone came from quarries under the city from its birth, later used for water, rubbish pits and as a war shelter.
quote: The circumstance that the city rests on tufaceous soil has favored practices of raising existing buildings, drawing the material from the underground quarries already used since the first birth of the city.
Shows former stone quarries, used the city buildings, transformed later to water distribution network, garbage disposal pits and finally a war shelter.

materials.label: verified
materials.says: Local materials give the city its look: yellow tufa, white marble and grey piperno, still used in restoration.
quote: There is remarkable continuity in the use of materials, all derived locally, and distinctive visual and material features, such as the basic yellow tufa, white marble, and the grey piperno

materials-now.label: verified
materials-now.says: The old techniques for these materials survive and are used in restoration.
quote: The techniques developed for the use of these materials survive to a considerable degree and are used in restoration and conservation projects.

churches-200.label: supported
churches-200.says: The ancient centre has more than 200 historic churches, linked to artists including Giotto, Caravaggio, Donatello and Giuseppe Sanmartino.
quote: sees the existence of more than 200 historic churches to which the activity of famous exponents of Italian art are linked. Among the main artists there are: Giotto, Caravaggio, Donatello, Giuseppe Sanmartino

domenico.label: supported
domenico.says: San Domenico Maggiore is a Gothic church founded in 1283 over a 10th-century church; its monastery was the first seat of the University of Naples, where Thomas Aquinas returned to teach theology in 1272, and Giordano Bruno lived there.
quote: This Gothic church (est. 1283) incorporates a smaller, original church built on this site in the 10th century

It was the original seat of the University of Naples, where Thomas Aquinas, a former monk at San Domenico Maggiore, returned to teach theology in 1272. As well, the philosopher monk, Giordano Bruno, lived here.

domenico-tombs.label: supported
domenico-tombs.says: The sacristy holds 45 tombs of the royal Aragonese family.
quote: The sacristy houses a series of 45 sepulchres of members of the royal Aragonese family, including that of King Ferdinand I.

duomo-end.label: supported
duomo-end.says: After crossing Via Duomo, Spaccanapoli loses much of its character and continues as Via Vicaria Vecchia.
quote: After crossing Via Duomo it loses much of its character, but continues east under the name Via Vicaria Vecchia.

living.label: verified
living.says: UNESCO stresses that Naples keeps its street pattern, historic buildings and the continuation of many of its urban and social functions.
quote: whose current urban fabric preserves a selection of outstanding elements of its long and eventful history, as expressed in its street pattern, its wealth of historic buildings and parks, the continuation of many of its urban and social functions

parts.name: Piazza del Gesù Nuovo
parts.stand: In the middle of Piazza del Gesù Nuovo, beside the tall carved spire, facing the church with the studded stone front.

paras.t: Welcome to the old heart of Naples, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1995. The street that runs past Santa Chiara, across the square, is Spaccanapoli. The name literally means Naples splitter.

Three landmarks share this square: the spire beside you, the church of Gesù Nuovo in front of you, and Santa Chiara across the way. And Spaccanapoli is only a nickname: on the signs you'll read Via Benedetto Croce, and further on, Via San Biagio dei Librai.

Look up at the spire. It's the Guglia dell'Immacolata, the tallest and most ornate of three plague columns in Naples. It is said it was built to ask the Virgin Mary for protection from the plague. It took its time, too: begun in the 1600s, and finished only in 1750, after decades of pauses.

Now look at the church front, covered in stone points. That's Gesù Nuovo, the New Jesus. And those diamond-shaped stones were never meant for a church. This was a palace, built in 1470 for Roberto Sanseverino, Prince of Salerno. His family got tangled in political intrigue, the property was confiscated, and in the 1580s the Jesuits bought it for 45,000 ducats. They built their church inside, and kept the palace front.

If you step inside, turn around once you're through the door. On the inside of the front wall is a huge painting, The Expulsion of Heliodorus from the Temple, by Francesco Solimena, from 1725. And in the chapel of the Visitation, under the altar, lies a doctor: Saint Joseph Moscati, who taught at the University of Naples and was head physician of the hospital of the Incurables. He died in 1927, and Pope John Paul the Second made him a saint in 1987.
Before we walk: Spaccanapoli is narrow and busy. Keep to the side, watch for scooters, mind the uneven paving, and keep your bag in front of you.

parts.name: Santa Chiara
parts.stand: Cross the square to the plain stone front of Santa Chiara, diagonally across from Gesù Nuovo.

paras.t: Santa Chiara looks severe after the Gesù. It's Gothic, built by King Robert of Naples and his queen, Sancha of Majorca. The exact dates differ from one account to another: 1310 to 1328 in one, 1313 to 1340 in another. Either way, it was the largest church of the Poor Clares ever built.

Inside, walk up toward the high altar. Right behind it is the tomb of King Robert of Anjou himself, carved by Pacio and Giovanni Bertini in 1343. And behind the tomb is a wall. It hides the nuns' choir, with three screened grilles. Through them the nuns could follow the Mass, while nobody in the church could see them.

Almost everything you see in here is a rebuilding. In 1943, Allied bombing and the fire that followed wrecked the church. It was brought back to a Gothic look by a restoration finished in 1953, and that restoration is still argued over. But for Naples, rebuilding Santa Chiara became the symbol of the city's rebirth.

In the side chapels are royal tombs: Francis the Second, Bourbon king of Naples, and his queen, Maria Sophie. And there's a quieter grave: Salvo D'Acquisto, a carabiniere who gave his life to save 22 civilian hostages during the Nazi occupation. He's remembered as a national hero.

If it's open, go round to the cloister at the back. In 1742 Domenico Antonio Vaccaro covered the nuns' cloister in majolica tiles, bright flowers on octagonal columns. It seems almost too cheerful for an enclosed convent, and that's part of the surprise.

parts.name: Along Spaccanapoli
parts.stand: Walk east along Via Benedetto Croce and stop where you can look straight down the length of the street.

paras.t: Look down the street. See how straight it is, in a city of small, irregular alleys? You're walking on a Greek plan. The rectangular grid of ancient Neapolis, the New City, can still be traced, and it still gives the old center its basic shape.

When was Neapolis founded? UNESCO dates it to 470 BC, refounded from an older settlement called Parthenope. Other accounts put the refounding in the 500s BC. Historians differ on the detail, but either way, the history of this old center spans more than 2,700 years.

Now look up. The buildings are tall and pressed together. In the Middle Ages the city was closed in by its walls, and building outside them was forbidden. So Naples grew upward instead of outward. Look at the stone, too: yellow tufa, white marble, and a grey stone called piperno, all local. The old ways of working them are still used in restoration today.

Under your feet there's a second city. Naples sits on tuff, and from its very beginning builders quarried their stone from underneath it. Later those hollows became part of the water system, then rubbish pits, and in the war, shelters. You can visit parts of them on underground tours.

The numbers in this old core are hard to take in. More than 200 historic churches. Giotto, Caravaggio, Donatello and Giuseppe Sanmartino all left work here. You can meet Sanmartino's most famous piece, the Veiled Christ, in the Sansevero Chapel.

parts.name: San Domenico Maggiore
parts.stand: In Piazza San Domenico Maggiore, facing the church.

paras.t: This is San Domenico Maggiore, a Gothic church founded in 1283, on top of a smaller church from the 10th century. Its monastery was the first home of the University of Naples. The great theologian Thomas Aquinas, once a monk here, came back to teach theology in 1272. The philosopher Giordano Bruno lived here too.
Kings are here as well. In the sacristy are 45 tombs of the royal Aragonese family.

parts.name: Via Duomo
parts.stand: Keep walking east until the street meets the wide cross street, Via Duomo, and turn to look back the way you came.

paras.t: Here at Via Duomo, our street changes its name to Via Vicaria Vecchia and loses much of its character. So this is a good place to turn around and look back.

UNESCO says what makes Naples special isn't only its monuments. It's that the city kept living in them: the same street pattern, the same buildings, many of the same everyday uses. Greek settlers drew this line. And for all the centuries since, the people of Naples have simply kept walking it.
